newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, Canada vow to double trade by 2000.
newsitem.headline: France, Canada vow to double trade by 2000.

text.p: France and Canada signed a partnership deal on Wednesday aimed at doubling economic, industrial and trade exchanges by the year 2000.

The deal, signed after talks between vsiiting Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien and French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, placed the emphasis on communications technology, including the development of the French language on the information highways.

The two countries also undertook to boost regular contacts between their leaders and develop cooperation on international issues such as the reform of the United Nations and NATO with a view to developing European defence within the Atlantic alliance.
Both members of the G7 group of industrialised countries, they also pledged to work closely together on solving regional crises and pushing for development aid to poor countries.
Chretien, who is on a three-day official visit, and Juppe told reporters they saw eye-to-eye on virtually all issues save for a disagreement on asbestos.

Canada, the world's second-biggest producer of asbestos, is pressing France to go back on its decision to ban all use of the fibre. Juppe promised his government would study a report playing down the risk of asbestos submitted by Canadian Industry Minister John Manley.
But the French prime minister said that he was not convinced. "When scientists do not agree, I set myself the rule of following the most cautious opinion," he said.
"We must continue trying to find a solution," said Chretien.
He said historical ties and common interests tied to the French language made France and Canada natural allies.

Juppe reaffirmed that Paris had no intention of interfering on the issue of the mainly French-speaking Quebec province. The risk of the province separating from Canada, with the possible encouragement of France, is a constant concern for Ottawa.

Earlier, Chretien made his first public stop at the Paris City Hall, telling Paris mayor Jean Tiberi that modern challenges, including unemployment, must be met with creativity and imagination and a reorganisation of resources.
"Part of the solution lies in our ability to expand our economic and trade cooperation," he said in an address delivered partly in French and partly in English.
He said the goal of doubling bilateral trade was fixed as a follow-up to proposals he made during a 1994 visit to Paris to boost exchanges and liberalise trade with Europe and Asia.
Diplomats said they expected deals to be announced between French and Canadian high-technology companies, including the space, computer and broadcasting industries.
Chretien hailed La Francophonie, the club of French-speaking countries, as an organisation for international cooperation.

He said Montreal would host a major Francophonie conference in May on the information highways, and Canada hoped to host the 1999 Francophonie summit in Moncton, New Brunswick. The 1997 summit is scheduled in Hanoi.
Chretien was returning Juppe's visit to Canada last June. He was due to have lunch with President Jacques Chirac on Thursday.
